title: Trump Signs GENIUS Stablecoin Act While Family-Linked USD1 Operates in Regulated Market
description_short: Trump Signs GENIUS Stablecoin Act While Family-Linked USD1 Operates in Regulated Market
description_medium: Trump signed the GENIUS Act on July 18, 2025, establishing a federal regulatory framework for payment stablecoins after a 68-30 Senate vote on June 17. By then, World Liberty Financial, a Trump-family-linked crypto venture, had launched USD1, and an Abu Dhabi-backed firm had selected USD1 to settle a $2 billion investment in Binance. Critics cited the president's financial ties as a conflict concern; the law did not bar the president or his family from stablecoin interests.
description_long: Trump signed the GENIUS Act on July 18, 2025, after the Senate approved it 68–30 on June 17. The law created a federal regulatory framework for payment stablecoins. At the same time, World Liberty Financial, a Trump-family-linked venture, had introduced its USD1 stablecoin, and an Abu Dhabi-backed firm selected USD1 to settle a $2 billion investment in Binance. These developments placed the president's legislative role alongside his family's financial connections to the industry being regulated. Critics identified that overlap as a conflict-of-interest concern. The supplied correction also notes that the law did not prohibit the president or his family from holding stablecoin interests. That is a supported description of the law's limits, not a finding that a specific transaction bought the legislation. The record establishes the enactment timeline, the Senate vote and the USD1 transaction connection. It does not establish an adjudicated corruption finding or quantify the family's profit from passage of the act.

title: Trump Taj Mahal Owed Contractors Tens of Millions After Opening
description_short: Trump Taj Mahal Owed Contractors Tens of Millions After Opening
description_medium: Fourteen weeks after the Trump Taj Mahal opened in Atlantic City, The Washington Post reported that unpaid bills were approaching $90 million. An attorney for a contractor said $72.8 million was owed to construction firms, and about 70 contractors were preparing to meet over whether to continue negotiations or sue. The record supports a substantial unpaid-contractor dispute at the Taj Mahal, but not the stored Trump Plaza/1992 framing or a blanket finding of fraud across Trump properties.
description_long: Fourteen weeks after the Trump Taj Mahal opened in Atlantic City, the Washington Post reported that unpaid bills were approaching $90 million. An attorney for a contractor said construction firms were owed $72.8 million, and roughly 70 contractors were preparing to meet to decide whether to continue negotiations or pursue litigation. The figures describe a substantial dispute over payment for work on the casino, with the narrower construction-firm amount attributed to the attorney. They are not interchangeable estimates of damages established by a court. The corrected reporting places this episode in July 1990 and identifies the Taj Mahal, rather than Trump Plaza in 1992. That distinction matters because the older framing attached the dispute to the wrong property and period. The supported event is contractors seeking payment and weighing their options. The supplied source does not establish a blanket finding of fraud across Trump's businesses or supply final outcomes for every contractor involved.
